title: Google patent describes an AI TV channel that casts you as the star
excerpt: Google My Channel would build videos from your watch history, location and age, with ads, and could use your face. The application was rejected.
content_html:
Google has described a TV channel that would generate AI videos for each viewer and could cast the viewer as the lead. The idea is set out in a patent application that Google filed in May 2025. The US Patent and Trademark Office published it on 19 November.

Its title is “Creating a Channel of Video Experiences Tailored to a User.” The patent tracker Patentlyze spotted it first and shared it with 404 Media. The examiner has issued a final rejection, Patentlyze reported, but Google can still amend the claims or appeal.

How “My Channel” would work

The filing describes a “My Channel” option in a TV app. A server gathers three kinds of data. One is what the user watches. Another is context from the device, such as its IP address, language setting or GPS location. The third is demographic data, such as an age bracket. The server turns them into a prompt for a large language model, which makes the videos.

The drawings show a home screen called “John’s Channel.” Its tiles offer a crime caper, a romantic comedy, a sci-fi adventure and an action thriller. New videos could arrive on a weekly, monthly or yearly timer, or on request.

One sample prompt in the filing, quoted by 404 Media, spells out the goal.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” the prompt reads.

Another example imagines a cricket fan who has been watching highlights of a player. The video could show the fan cheering for India in the stands.

Your face, your voice, and ads

In the fuller version, the system builds an avatar from the user’s photos. It could also keep audio from TV voice commands. Mashable found that the filing would use it to “synthesize the voice of the user for the dialogue of a protagonist.”

Ads are part of the design. An “advertising stitcher” would insert at least one advertisement into each customized video before it plays, according to the filing.

The filing says users can control what data the system collects. Users who share less data would get more generic results, Patentlyze noted.

Google did not respond to requests for comment from Gizmodo and CNET, and it has not announced a product. YouTube already lets users build custom AI feeds of existing videos. Other platforms are moving the other way. Tidal is removing AI-generated tracks, and Spotify pulled 50 million AI tracks.

Published November 26, 2026 - 4:43 pm UTC
